Consider contiguous allocation of physical memory to processes using variable partitioning scheme. Suppose there are [latex]8[/latex] holes in the memory of sizes [latex]20 \text{KB}, 4 \text{KB}[/latex], [latex]25 \text{KB}, 18 \text{KB}, 7 \text{KB}, 9 \text{KB}, 15 \text{KB}[/latex], and [latex]12\text{KB}[/latex]. Assume that no two holes are adjacent. Two processes [latex]\text{P1}[/latex] of size [latex]16KB[/latex] and [latex]\text{P2}[/latex] of size [latex]9KB[/latex] arrive in that order, and they are allocated memory using the best-fit technique. After allocating space to [latex]\text{P1}[/latex] and [latex]\text{P2}[/latex], the number of holes of size less than [latex]8KB[/latex] is ________. (answer in integer)
Note: [latex]1 {K}=2^{10}[/latex]
solution:
Best-fit always picks the smallest hole that is still large enough to satisfy the request.

Initial holes (KB): [latex]20,4,25,18,7,9,15,12[/latex].

P1 (16 KB): smallest hole [latex]\ge16[/latex] is [latex]18[/latex]. Allocate there, leaving a remainder hole of [latex]18-16=2[/latex] KB. Holes become: [latex]20,4,25,7,9,15,12,2[/latex].

P2 (9 KB): smallest hole [latex]\ge9[/latex] is the exact-fit [latex]9[/latex] KB hole itself, which is fully consumed (disappears entirely). Holes become: [latex]20,4,25,7,15,12,2[/latex] ([latex]7[/latex] holes remaining).

Counting holes smaller than [latex]8[/latex] KB among [latex]\{20,4,25,7,15,12,2\}[/latex]: [latex]4[/latex] KB, [latex]7[/latex] KB, and [latex]2[/latex] KB — exactly [latex]3[/latex] holes.

Answer: 3

text: Which one of the following CPU scheduling algorithms cannot be preemptive?
solution:
Checking whether each scheduling algorithm supports preemption:

- SRTF is explicitly the preemptive version of Shortest-Job-First — it can preempt a running process whenever a newly arrived process has a shorter remaining time.
- Round Robin is inherently preemptive — it forcibly preempts a running process once its time quantum expires.
- Priority Scheduling can be implemented in either a preemptive form (a higher-priority arrival preempts the current process) or non-preemptive form — so it certainly can be preemptive.
- FCFS (First Come First Serve) is defined by running processes strictly to completion in arrival order — there is no mechanism within FCFS for a later-arriving process to interrupt/preempt the one currently executing. It is inherently non-preemptive by definition.

Answer: First Come First Serve (FCFS) Scheduling cannot be preemptive.

text:
Consider a system that has a cache memory unit and a memory management unit (MMU). The address input to the cache memory is a physical address. The MMU has a translation lookaside buffer (TLB). Assume that when a page is evicted from the main memory, the corresponding blocks in the cache are marked as invalid.

For a given memory reference, which of the following sequences of events can NEVER happen?
solution:
A memory reference passes through, in order: TLB → (page table, only if TLB misses) → cache.

- TLB miss, Page table hit, Cache hit: possible — TLB doesn't have the mapping, page table does (page is in memory), and the corresponding cache block (whose validity depends on the page being resident) can indeed be valid and hit. Can happen.
- TLB hit, Page table miss, Cache hit: impossible. A TLB hit means the page is currently mapped/resident in memory (TLB entries are only valid for pages currently in memory); it is therefore contradictory for the page table to then report a miss (page not in memory) for that very same page.
- TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache hit: impossible. A page-table miss means the page is not in main memory at all — and the problem states that when a page is evicted, its cache blocks are marked invalid. So if the page isn't in memory, its cache blocks cannot be valid, and a cache hit is impossible.
- TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache miss: possible and in fact the expected/consistent sequence when a page is genuinely not resident.

Answer: "TLB hit, Page table miss, Cache hit" and "TLB miss, Page table miss, Cache hit" can NEVER happen.

text:
Consider a system consisting of [latex]k[/latex] instances of a resource [latex]R[/latex], being shared by [latex]5[/latex] processes. Assume that each process requires a maximum of two instances of resource [latex]R[/latex] and a process can request or release only one instance at a time. Further, a process can request the second instance of the resource only after acquiring the first instance.

The minimum value of [latex]k[/latex] for the system to be deadlock-free is ________. (answer in integer)
solution:
This is the classic deadlock-avoidance-by-resource-count formula. Each of the [latex]5[/latex] processes needs at most [latex]2[/latex] instances of [latex]R[/latex].

A guaranteed deadlock-free allocation is possible if, even in the worst case where every process is holding one instance and waiting for its second, at least one process can still obtain its second instance and finish (then release both, allowing the rest to proceed in turn).

Worst case: each of the [latex]5[/latex] processes holds [latex](max-1)=1[/latex] instance already, using up [latex]5\times1=5[/latex] instances, and one more instance must be available so that at least one waiting process can get its 2nd instance and complete.

So minimum [latex]k=5\times(2-1)+1=6[/latex].

Answer: 6

text: With respect to deadlocks in an operating system, which of the following statements is/are FALSE?
solution:
Evaluating each deadlock-related statement:

- "Banker's algorithm is used to prevent deadlocks" — FALSE. Banker's algorithm is a deadlock-avoidance algorithm (it checks resource requests dynamically to keep the system in a safe state); deadlock prevention refers to a different set of techniques that structurally rule out one of the four necessary conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no pre-emption, circular wait).
- "Deadlock formation can be prevented by disallowing hold-and-wait" — true: this is a standard, valid deadlock-prevention technique (one of the four necessary conditions is removed).
- "An assignment edge in a resource-allocation graph is marked from a process to a resource" — FALSE. It's the reverse: an assignment edge goes from a resource to a process (resource is allocated to the process); a request edge goes from a process to a resource.
- "A safe state guarantees all processes can finish without deadlock" — true: this is precisely the definition of a safe state.

Answer (the FALSE statements): "Banker's algorithm prevents deadlocks", and "an assignment edge goes from process to resource."

A computer system supports a logical address space of [latex]2^{32}[/latex] bytes. It uses two-level hierarchical paging with a page size of 4096 bytes. A logical address is divided into a [latex]b[/latex]-bit index to the outer page table, an offset within the page of the inner page table, and an offset within the desired page. Each entry of the inner page table uses eight bytes. All the pages in the system have the same size.

The value of [latex]b[/latex] is ___________ . (Answer in integer)
solution:
Page size [latex]=4096=2^{12}[/latex] bytes, so the page offset needs [latex]12[/latex] bits. Logical address space [latex]=2^{32}[/latex] bytes, so the remaining [latex]32-12=20[/latex] bits form the combined page-number field, split between the outer index ([latex]b[/latex] bits) and the inner-page-table offset.

Since each inner page table must itself fit exactly within one page (standard assumption for multi-level paging), and each entry is [latex]8[/latex] bytes, the inner page table holds [latex]\dfrac{4096}{8}=512=2^9[/latex] entries — so the inner-table offset field needs [latex]9[/latex] bits.

[latex]b=20-9=11[/latex]

Answer: 11

[latex]P = \{P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4\} [/latex] consists of all active processes in an operating system. [latex]R = \{R_1, R_2, R_3, R_4\} [/latex] consists of single instances of distinct types of resources in the system.
The resource allocation graph has the following assignment and claim edges.

[latex] \text{Assignment edges: } R_1 \to P_1, R_2 \to P_2, R_3 \to P_3, R_4 \to P_4 [/latex] (the assignment edge [latex]R_1 \to P_1[/latex] means resource [latex]R_1[/latex] is assigned to process [latex]P_1[/latex], and so on for others)

[latex] \text{Claim edges: } P_1 \to R_2, P_2 \to R_3, P_3 \to R_1, P_2 \to R_4, P_4 \to R_2 [/latex] (the claim edge [latex]P_1 \to R_2[/latex] means process [latex]P_1[/latex] is waiting for resource [latex]R_2[/latex], and so on for others)

Which of the following statement(s) is/are CORRECT?
solution:
Build the resource-allocation graph and look for cycles (with single-instance resources, a cycle means deadlock):

Cycle A: [latex]P_1\to R_2\to P_2\to R_3\to P_3\to R_1\to P_1[/latex] (involving [latex]P_1,P_2,P_3[/latex]).
Cycle B: [latex]P_2\to R_4\to P_4\to R_2\to P_2[/latex] (involving [latex]P_2,P_4[/latex]).

Both cycles share [latex]P_2[/latex] as a common process. Aborting [latex]P_2[/latex] alone breaks both cycles simultaneously (removing [latex]P_2[/latex]'s edges collapses both cycles at once) — system becomes deadlock-free.

Aborting [latex]P_1[/latex] alone only breaks Cycle A; Cycle B (which never involved [latex]P_1[/latex]) remains fully intact — still deadlocked. Similarly, aborting [latex]P_3[/latex] alone only touches Cycle A, leaving Cycle B untouched — still deadlocked.

Aborting both [latex]P_1[/latex] and [latex]P_4[/latex] together: removing [latex]P_1[/latex] frees [latex]R_1[/latex] (letting [latex]P_3[/latex]'s wait resolve), and removing [latex]P_4[/latex] frees [latex]R_4[/latex] (letting [latex]P_2[/latex]'s wait for [latex]R_4[/latex] resolve); with both freed, the remaining chain ([latex]P_2,P_3[/latex]) can fully unwind — deadlock-free.

Answer: Aborting P2 alone works; and aborting both P1 and P4 together works.

text:
A computer has two processors, [latex]M_1[/latex] and [latex]M_2[/latex]. Four processes [latex]P_1, P_2, P_3, P_4[/latex] with CPU bursts of 20, 16, 25, and 10 milliseconds, respectively, arrive at the same time and these are the only processes in the system. The scheduler uses non-preemptive priority scheduling, with priorities decided as follows:

[latex]M_1[/latex] uses priority of execution for the processes as, [latex]P_1 > P_3 > P_2 > P_4[/latex], i.e., [latex]P_1[/latex] and [latex]P_4[/latex] have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.
[latex]M_2[/latex] uses priority of execution for the processes as, [latex]P_2 > P_3 > P_4 > P_1[/latex], i.e., [latex]P_2[/latex] and [latex]P_1[/latex] have highest and lowest priorities, respectively.

A process [latex]P_i[/latex] is scheduled to a processor [latex]M_k[/latex], if the processor is free and no other process [latex]P_j[/latex] is waiting with higher priority. At any given point of time, a process can be allocated to any one of the free processors without violating the execution priority rules. Ignore the context switch time. What will be the average waiting time of the processes in milliseconds?
solution:
All four processes arrive together at [latex]t=0[/latex] with two free processors, so two of them start immediately. Since [latex]P_1[/latex] is [latex]M_1[/latex]'s top priority and [latex]P_2[/latex] is [latex]M_2[/latex]'s top priority (and conveniently each is the other machine's lowest priority, so there's no conflict), the natural non-conflicting start is [latex]P_1\to M_1[/latex] and [latex]P_2\to M_2[/latex], both beginning at [latex]t=0[/latex].
